name: Lod
founded_note: Ancient town (Lydda); CBS dates the Israeli locality to 1948.

status.note: Allotted to the Arab state by the 1947 partition plan; held by local defenders with Arab Legion (Transjordan) units until Operation Dani.

cite.claim: Lod was held with Transjordan's Arab Legion
cite.quote: When the resolution was rejected by the Arab states, Lod was occupied by the invading Arab Legion of Jordan.

cite.claim: Lydda and Ramle: Ben-Gurion wanted them 'destroyed'; Arab Legion troops present in July 1948
cite.quote: Repeatedly he jotted down in his diary that Lydda and Ramle had to be ‘destroyed’ ... the presence in them of Arab Legion troops implied a commitment by King Abdullah to their defence

cite.claim: Population of Lydda and Ramle together in July 1948 (Morris's estimate)
cite.quote: Lydda and Ramle had to be ‘destroyed’ ... In July 1948, the two towns together had a population of roughly 50,000–70,000, of whom 20,000 or so were refugees from Jaffa and its environs

status.note: Captured in Operation Dani on 11-12 July 1948. name: Abu Ghosh
founded_note: Arab village west of Jerusalem whose residents largely remained in 1948.

status.note: Village on the Tel Aviv-Jerusalem road; its villagers kept friendly relations with the Jewish side (some cooperated with the Haganah and Lehi). Morris (2004) records that it was exempted from the clearing of Arab communities along that road, but that on 13 July 1948 the IDF Chief of General Staff complained of a report that the Harel Brigade commander had ordered the Arabs of Abu Gosh to evacuate and reiterated that such orders needed the defence minister's authorisation. Israel National News reports that residents received eviction notices after 1948 but, after public protest, most were allowed to resettle by 1950; an opinion piece in +972 Magazine states that many families became refugees in Jordan in 1948. No source consulted gives the number of residents who left or returned.

status.note: Captured by Israel in the Six-Day War (June 1967) and placed under Israeli military administration. Much of the town was demolished and its residents were temporarily displaced: according to the UN Secretary-General's Special Representative (report A/6797, Sept. 1967), Qalqilya was a town of some 13,000 to 14,000 inhabitants; Jordanian complaints to the Security Council claimed that 12,000 people from Qalqilya were living in the open around 22 June. The Arab mayor told the Special Representative's assistant that most residents had left before and during the fighting and about one quarter remained; the remaining population was advised by the Israeli military commander to leave, was taken to Azun and then Nablus, and was allowed back after three weeks, finding about 850 of some 2,000 dwellings demolished. The Israeli military governor said the destruction was caused partly by tanks and partly by dynamite (houses used for sniping, and others for safety or sanitary reasons); Israel's letter to the Security Council (S/8013) said Qalqilya was a concentration point of the Jordanian attack, that the inhabitants left before Israeli troops arrived, and that only houses where Jordanian troops were found were damaged. Affected populations: the Palestinian (Jordanian-administered West Bank) residents of Qalqilya, plus residents of nearby villages such as Beit Awa and Beit Mersim, which the same report records as demolished; the Israeli and Jordanian sources differ on the cause and extent of the destruction.

name: Jaffa
founded_note: Ancient port city (Jaffa / Yafo); the largest Arab city in Mandatory Palestine. Merged into Tel Aviv in 1950 (see tel_aviv).

status.note: Arab-majority city; fighting around Jaffa followed the UN partition vote of 29 November 1947. Its Arab defenders capitulated on 13 May 1948.

cite.claim: Before 1948 Jaffa was a largely Arab city (about 70,000 of nearly 100,000 non-Jews, 1946-47)
cite.quote: 70,000 were non-Jews, making Jaffa the largest Arab city in the country.

status.note: Fell to Jewish forces on 13 May 1948 (capitulation signed at Tel Aviv Haganah headquarters; sources date it 13 May, the day before the State was declared). The Encyclopaedia Judaica puts the Arab inhabitants at 100,000 and those remaining in summer 1948 at about 4,000; the Jewish Virtual Library says most abandoned the city by sea. Palestinian and Israeli accounts differ on flight versus expulsion.

cite.claim: About 4,000 of Jaffa's 100,000 Arab inhabitants remained in summer 1948 (EJ)
cite.quote: The flight of most of Jaffa's 100,000 Arab inhabitants (of whom only 4,000 remained in the summer of 1948

cite.claim: Capitulation signed 13 May 1948 (EJ, Tel Aviv-Jaffa entry)
cite.quote: the signing of its capitulation in the Tel Aviv Haganah headquarters on May 13, 1948
cite.covers: same EJ entry as the quote naming Jaffa's 100,000 Arab inhabitants; the capitulation line describes Jaffa's surrender

cite.claim: On May 13, 1948 Jaffa fell to Jewish forces and most of its inhabitants left by sea (JVL)
cite.quote: On May 13, 1948, the city fell to Jewish forces, and most of its inhabitants abandoned it by sea.
cite.covers: Jewish Virtual Library 'Jaffa' article; the sentence describes Jaffa's fall

status.note: Merged with Tel Aviv in 1950 and the record ends here (merged_into tel_aviv). The Israeli government decided on 4 October 1949 to amalgamate the two; the Jewish Virtual Library says they were officially combined in 1950 and named Tel Aviv-Jaffa a year after the decision. The exact day (24 April 1950 is often given) was not confirmed in a non-Wikipedia source.

cite.claim: Jaffa and Tel Aviv combined into one city in 1950
cite.quote: In 1950, Jaffa and Tel Aviv were officially combined into one city.

cite.claim: Government decision of 4 Oct 1949 to amalgamate Tel Aviv with Jaffa; renamed a year later
cite.quote: on Oct. 4, 1949, the government of Israel decided to amalgamate Tel Aviv with Jaffa, which one year later were given the name Tel Aviv-Jaffa

cite.claim: In 1950, following the repopulation of Jaffa, the two cities were united
cite.quote: In 1950, consequent upon the repopulation of Jaffa, both cities were united to form the Israeli metropolis of Tel Aviv-Jaffa.

population_notes.1947: approx. non-Jewish (Arab) residents of a city of nearly 100,000 in 1946-47 (Jewish Virtual Library)
population_notes.1948: Arab inhabitants remaining in summer 1948 (Encyclopaedia Judaica: of about 100,000 Arab inhabitants; 2,000 Muslim, 1,500 Christian, rest Armenian and others)

population_comment: Sources differ on the pre-war Arab population: the Jewish Virtual Library gives about 70,000 non-Jews in a city of nearly 100,000 (1946-47), while the Encyclopaedia Judaica speaks of 100,000 Arab inhabitants. Both agree that most left in the first half of 1948 (Encyclopaedia Judaica: only about 4,000 remained in summer 1948; Jewish Virtual Library: most abandoned the city by sea after its fall on 13 May 1948). Palestinian and Israeli accounts differ on how far the departure was flight and how far expulsion; these sources give no figure for the number expelled.
notes: Record ends with the 1950 merger; see tel_aviv.

name: East Jerusalem
founded_note: The Old City and the Arab neighbourhoods north and east of it; part of ancient Jerusalem.

status.note: Intense fighting in the Old City began on 14 May 1948; Israeli attempts to break through Zion Gate failed.

cite.claim: Intense fighting in the Old City began on 14 May 1948; Israeli forces failed to take it
cite.quote: Intense fighting began in the Old City just after the establishment of the State of Israel on May 14, 1948.

status.note: Jordan's Arab Legion took the Jewish Quarter on 28 May 1948 and the Old City passed to Jordanian control.

cite.claim: Jewish Quarter fell to Jordan's Arab Legion on 28 May 1948
cite.quote: Jordan's Arab Legion continued to capture more and more of the Jewish Quarter - until the fateful Friday, May 28, when the Jewish Quarter fell.

cite.claim: Surrender papers signed, giving Jerusalem over to Jordanian control
cite.quote: the official surrender papers were signed, giving Jerusalem over to Jordanian control.
cite.covers: same article passage as the Jewish Quarter (Old City) quote; describes the Old City passing to Jordan

status.note: Administered by Jordan under the 1949 armistice (Jordan annexed the West Bank including East Jerusalem in April 1950, recognised by few states).

cite.claim: Parts of Jerusalem including the Old City were under Jordanian rule 1948-67
cite.quote: those parts of Jerusalem that had been under Jordanian rule from 1948 to 1967, including the Old City

cite.claim: Ostteil (East Jerusalem) incl. Altstadt was Jordanian-controlled after the war
cite.quote: Während der Westteil zu Israel kam, war der Ostteil jordanisch kontrolliert. Dazu gehörte die Altstadt

cite.claim: Armistice lines in the Jerusalem sector follow the 30 Nov 1948 cease-fire lines
cite.quote: In the Jerusalem sector, the Armistice Demarcation Lines shall correspond to the lines defined in the 30 November 1948 Cease-Fire Agreement for the Jerusalem area
cite.covers: Article V of the Israel-Jordan armistice (3 April 1949) fixed the Jerusalem line that left the Old City and East Jerusalem with Jordan

status.note: Israeli law, jurisdiction and administration extended to East Jerusalem on 27-28 June 1967; Basic Law: Jerusalem (1980). The UN Security Council (Res. 478) held the 1980 law null and void; most states do not recognise the annexation.

cite.claim: 27-28 June 1967: Israeli law extended and new municipal boundaries proclaimed, incorporating the Old City
cite.quote: the Israeli government proclaimed new municipal boundaries for the city of Jerusalem, incorporating within the limits of the unified city, inter alia, those parts of Jerusalem that had been under Jordanian rule from 1948 to 1967, including the Old City.

cite.claim: Israel's aim since occupying East Jerusalem in June 1967 was sovereignty over the whole city
cite.quote: Since the day it occupied East Jerusalem in June 1967, Israel had one overriding goal: to secure Israeli sovereignty over the entire city.

cite.claim: Basic Law: Jerusalem, Capital of Israel (30 July 1980)
cite.quote: 1. Jerusalem, complete and united, is the capital of Israel. ... * Passed by the Knesset on the 17th Av, 5740 (30th July, 1980)
cite.covers: the Basic Law applies to the unified city including East Jerusalem and the Old City

cite.claim: UN Security Council Res. 478 (1980) censured the Basic Law as null and void
cite.quote: Resolution 478 (1980) of 20 August 1980 ... 1. Censures in the strongest terms the enactment by Israel of the "basic law" on Jerusalem ... are null and void and must be rescinded forthwith
cite.covers: resolution on the 1980 Basic Law applying to East Jerusalem
